Remove the atom at one selected lattice site to create a vacancy defect.
Replace the atom at one selected lattice site with a specified element.
Insert an additional atom at specified fractional or Cartesian coordinates.
Exchange the species on two selected lattice sites to create an antisite pair.
No additional parameters are required for this operation.
Selected atoms move together so their mean fractional position reaches the target. Unwrap selections that cross a periodic boundary first.
Symbols: Δf is the common fractional translation; ftarget is the target; fi is atom i's original fractional position; N is the number of selected atoms.
Sites within the periodic minimum-image tolerance are moved to their mean position. Delete keeps one site; Sum combines occupancies; Average averages compatible numeric properties.
The Cartesian normal and point define the mirror plane. Only selected atoms move; the lattice is unchanged.
$\hat{\mathbf n}=\frac{\mathbf n}{\|\mathbf n\|},\qquad \mathbf r^{\prime}=\mathbf r-2[(\mathbf r-\mathbf p)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}]\hat{\mathbf n}$
Symbols: r and r′ are the Cartesian positions before and after mirroring; p is a point on the plane; n is the plane normal; n̂ is its unit vector; · is the dot product.

Each affected atom receives a random direction and a displacement uniformly sampled between the minimum and maximum values. The seed makes the result reproducible. Both current perturb commands affect all atoms.
Axis and anchor are Cartesian; the anchor is in Å. Positive angles follow the right-hand rule. The lattice remains fixed and rotated atoms are wrapped into the cell.
Symbols: r and r′ are the Cartesian positions before and after rotation; p is the anchor; n̂ is the unit rotation axis; θ is the entered angle; R is the rotation matrix.
Cartesian vectors are in Å. Fractional vectors use the lattice basis: [1 0 0] translates by one complete a vector. Periodic results are wrapped into the cell.
A scalar acts on all axes; three values specify the axial strains. Fractional coordinates stay fixed. Shear strain is not supported.
Symbols: A and A′ are the lattice matrices before and after strain; εx, εy and εz are dimensionless axial strains. For example, 0.01 means 1% extension.
Matrix rows are a, b and c. Preserve Cartesian off keeps fractional coordinates, so atoms deform with the cell. On keeps Cartesian positions and recomputes fractional coordinates.
Symbols: A is the lattice matrix whose rows are a, b and c; f is a fractional-coordinate row vector; r is the corresponding Cartesian position.
The chosen basis vector is reversed while fractional coordinates stay fixed. Cartesian positions and basis handedness may change. This is not a spatial mirror of the atoms.
Symbols: ai and ai′ are the selected lattice vector before and after reversal; i is the chosen axis index.
The lattice and all atoms rotate together about the Cartesian axis. Lengths, angles and internal distances remain unchanged.
The value must permute 1, 2 and 3. [2 1 3] makes the new axes b, a and c and reorders fractional components to preserve Cartesian positions.
The input is an integer transformation. [2 2 2] gives an eightfold cell; nondiagonal matrices create tilted or reoriented supercells.
Symbols: S is the integer transformation; A and A′ are the original and new lattice matrices; N and N′ are their atom counts; |det S| is the cell-volume multiplier.
The lattice is replaced while Cartesian atomic positions stay fixed. Periodic images are not added or removed; choose a cell that contains the existing geometry.
This searches integer supercells whose angles are near 90° and whose lengths satisfy the bounds. Larger length and atom limits or a looser angle tolerance make a solution more likely.
Vacancy removes one site; substitution changes one species; interstitial adds an atom at the given coordinates; antisite exchanges the species on two sites.

SQS preserves a disordered alloy's composition while matching random-alloy pair correlations. Scalar k targets k times the cell volume, not k times each axis. Small spaces are enumerated; larger ones use a time-bounded Monte Carlo search.
The chiral vector becomes the circumference. For hexagonal layers, (n,0) is zigzag and (n,n) armchair. Axial repetitions set the periodic tube length.
Symbols: (n,m) are the chiral indices; a1 and a2 are the in-plane lattice vectors; Ch is the circumference vector; R is the tube radius.
Width is a number of transverse lattice repeats, not Å. Zigzag and armchair select different edge directions. Only the ribbon axis remains periodic.
The integer indices define the wire axis. Atoms are retained inside a Cartesian cylinder of the requested radius. Only the wire axis remains periodic.
Symbols: [u v w] are integer direction indices; a, b and c are lattice vectors; t is the Cartesian wire-axis vector.

Dot retains atoms inside a centered sphere and removes periodicity; vacuum surrounds the result. Void removes atoms inside a sphere centered at fractional [0.5 0.5 0.5] and keeps the original periodic cell.
The Miller indices define the surface normal in reciprocal space. Slab thickness is a minimum. Reducing the surface cell may change orientation and site ordering.
Symbols: (h k l) are Miller indices; b1, b2 and b3 are reciprocal-lattice vectors; Ghkl is normal to the selected surface.
This value is added to the third lattice-vector length; it is not the final vacuum thickness. Atoms are recentered along that vector, which is assumed to be the surface normal.
Symbols: c and c′ are the third lattice vector before and after the operation; Δ is the requested additional length in Å.
Gap is the separation between the facing atomic surfaces. Maximum strain limits in-plane mismatch. The input layers must already have identical or nearly matched in-plane cells.

Only hexagonal 2D primitive cells are supported. Integer coincidence cells are ranked by angle error, strain and atom count. A larger index may improve the angle match but increases size and search cost.
The count excludes fixed endpoints, which must have identical lattices, species and ordering. The IDPP force tolerance is not a physical first-principles force criterion.
Symbols: dij is the distance between atoms i and j in an image; d*ij is its interpolated target; EIDPP is the artificial path-smoothing objective.
Height places top, bridge and hollow candidates above the surface normal. It is not a predicted equilibrium bond length; relax candidate structures before use.

Under-coordinated atoms are detected with Jmol-radius neighbors inside the surface depth. Target 0 uses the largest observed coordination for each element; thin slabs may require an explicit target. Colliding placements are rejected.

Clearance starts the packing region above the surface; layer thickness sets its depth; vacuum separates it from the cell boundary. Packmol tolerance avoids overlaps but does not set physical liquid density.
Larger distance and angle tolerances usually detect higher symmetry but may hide real distortions. Standard primitive or conventional cells may change orientation, site order and site count.
